fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1689 (Sort Year: 1689)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Locke

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A letter arguing that the state must not force religious belief.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Liberty Fund dates the Latin writing to 1685 and publication to 1689. The English version also appeared in 1689.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: John Locke (The writer, addressing a friend on toleration)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Locke wrote the Latin letter in Holland in 1685.
It was published in 1689, then put into English by William Popple.
He calls toleration the mark of a true church.
The magistrate may guard peace and property, not souls.
True faith, he says, must be an inward persuasion.

items.title: "A Satire against Reason and Mankind" (1679) — John Wilmot, Earl of Rochester

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: A Satire against Reason and Mankind

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1679 (Sort Year: 1679)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Wilmot, Earl of Rochester

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A bitter poem that says human reason is a false guide and beasts are wiser.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: A manuscript copy is dated June 1674. Harold Love dates the first broadside (a single printed sheet) to 1679. Wing and the ESTC (old book catalogues) date one issue about 1675. The fuller poem appeared in 1680, in Poems on Several Occasions. That book pretends to be printed at Antwerp, but it was printed in London.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Speaker (A cynical court wit who attacks pride in reason); The Clergyman (A formal objector, called a band and beard in the poem)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The speaker wishes he were a dog, a monkey, or a bear.
He calls reason an ignis fatuus (a false fire) that leads people astray.
A clergyman objects, and the speaker answers him.
He says right reason should serve the senses and appetite.
He argues that fear, not virtue, drives most human honour.
He ends by saying people differ more from each other than from beasts.

items.title: "An Essay Concerning Human Understanding" (1689) — John Locke

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: An Essay Concerning Human Understanding

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1689 (Sort Year: 1689)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Locke

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A long essay arguing that ideas come from experience.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Drafts began in 1671. The book appeared in December 1689. The title page is dated 1690.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: John Locke (The philosopher arguing in his own voice)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Locke began drafts in 1671.
The book was published in December 1689, with 1690 on the title page.
He denies that the mind holds ideas from birth.
He asks us to picture the mind as white paper.
Sensation and reflection, he says, supply all our ideas.

items.title: "An Essay of Dramatic Poesy" (1668) — John Dryden

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: An Essay of Dramatic Poesy

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1668 (Sort Year: 1668)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Dryden

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Four friends debate ancient, French, and English drama on the day of a sea battle.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That is only the period mark. Plague closed the theatres in 1665, and Dryden wrote the essay then. It was printed in 1668.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Crites (Defends ancient drama. He is based on Sir Robert Howard.); Eugenius (Defends the moderns. He is based on Charles Sackville.); Lisideius (Praises French neoclassical plays. He is based on Sir Charles Sedley.); Neander (Stands for Dryden. He defends mixed plays, called tragicomedy, and Shakespeare.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The theatres were shut in 1665 because plague had hit London.
Dryden wrote this dialogue then, and it was printed in 1668.
Crites defends the ancient Greeks and Romans.
Eugenius defends modern writers, and Lisideius praises French rules.
Neander, who stands for Dryden, defends English plays and Shakespeare.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Diary

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1825 (Sort Year: 1825)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Samuel Pepys

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A secret diary of Restoration London, from court and navy office to plague and fire.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: He wrote from 1 January 1660 to 31 May 1669. Lord Braybrooke published a shortened text in 1825. The full edition by Robert Latham and William Matthews appeared in 1970-1983.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Samuel Pepys (The diarist, Clerk of the Acts and later a navy secretary); Elisabeth Pepys (His wife, often present in the domestic entries); Charles II (The restored king, whose return and court Pepys records)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Pepys began the diary on 1 January 1660.
He records the return of Charles II and his own rise at the Navy Board.
He describes the Great Plague of 1665 and the Great Fire of 1666.
He also notes plays, money, quarrels, and his home life.
He stopped on 31 May 1669, afraid that writing was hurting his eyes.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Hudibras

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1663 (Sort Year: 1663)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Samuel Butler (Restoration, 1613–1680)

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A comic epic that sends a Puritan knight on absurd adventures.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Part 1 appeared with a 1663 title page. Part 2 followed in 1664. Part 3 followed in 1678. Butler began the poem about 1658.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Sir Hudibras (A Presbyterian knight, pedantic and absurdly brave); Ralpho (His squire, an Independent who argues religion with him)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is a mock heroic narrative poem. It is a satire upon Roundheads, Presbyterians, Puritans, and many other factions involved in the English Civil War.
The work begun during the civil war and published in three parts in 1663, 1664, and 1678.
The epic tells the story of Sir Hudibras, a knight errant who is described dramatically and with laudatory praise.
He is praised for his knowledge of logic despite appearing stupid throughout but his religious fervor is mainly attacked.
The squire name of Sir Hudibras was Ralpho.
Voltaire in his "Letters on the English" said about Hudibras- "I never found so much wit in one single book."
In this poem, Butler has coined the phrase- "Spare the rod and spoil the child".
Sir Hudibras, a Presbyterian knight, rides out to reform the people.
His squire Ralpho is an Independent, so the two quarrel over doctrine.
They meet people dancing and baiting a bear.
The knight's learning is huge and useless.
The joke is that religious zeal looks like false chivalry.

items.title: "Love-Letters Between a Nobleman and His Sister" (1684) — Aphra Behn

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Love-Letters Between a Nobleman and His Sister

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1684 (Sort Year: 1684)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Aphra Behn

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A letter novel about an unlawful love, based on a London scandal.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Part one came out in 1684, part two in 1685, and part three in 1687. Britannica gives the span 1684-1687. The printed title joins Love and Letters with a hyphen. It was first printed without her name.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Silvia (A young woman based on Lady Henrietta Berkeley); Philander (Silvia's brother by marriage, based on Lord Grey); Octavio (A rich Dutch nobleman who loves Silvia); Cesario (A rebel prince standing for the Duke of Monmouth)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Silvia is wooed by Philander, the husband of her sister.
Their letters show the affair, and then the pair flee abroad.
In Holland, the nobleman Octavio falls in love with Silvia.
Philander grows faithless, and Silvia turns to schemes and revenge.
A side plot shows the rebel Cesario defeated and executed.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Lycidas

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1638 (Sort Year: 1638)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Milton

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A pastoral elegy mourning the drowning of Milton's college friend Edward King.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Lycidas was written in November 1637 and first published in Cambridge in 1638 in Justa Edovardo King naufrago.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Shepherd / Uncouth Swain (The grieving speaker who sings the elegy for his friend); Lycidas (The pastoral figure representing Edward King, who drowned at sea); Phoebus Apollo (The god of poetry who explains true fame in Heaven); Saint Peter / Pilot of the Galilean lake (The biblical figure who attacks corrupt clergy)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The shepherd speaker laments the early death of his fellow shepherd Lycidas.
He questions the water nymphs for failing to save his drowning friend.
He wonders why poets work hard if life can end so suddenly.
Saint Peter speaks and condemns corrupt, greedy church leaders.
The speaker concludes that Lycidas lives on in Heaven, and he moves on to new tasks.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Samson Agonistes

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1671 (Sort Year: 1671)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Milton

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A tragic closet drama about the biblical hero Samson in his final hours as a prisoner.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Samson Agonistes was first published in 1671 with Paradise Regained. It was never performed on stage in Milton's lifetime.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Samson (The blind Israelite champion held captive in Gaza); Manoah (Samson's aged father who attempts to ransom him); Dalila (Samson's Philistine wife who betrayed him); Harapha (A boastful Philistine giant who mocks Samson); Chorus of Danites (Samson's fellow Israelites who comment on the action)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Blind and captive Samson laments his fallen state while grinding corn for the Philistines.
His father Manoah visits and offers to pay a ransom for his release.
His treacherous wife Dalila visits and asks for forgiveness, but Samson firmly rejects her.
The Philistine giant Harapha taunts Samson, but Samson challenges him to fight.
Samson is led to the Philistine feast, where he pulls down the temple pillars and dies killing his enemies.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Pilgrim’s Progress

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1678 (Sort Year: 1678)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Bunyan

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Christian travels from the City of Destruction to the Celestial City.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Both are wrong. Part one was published in 1678. Part two was published in 1684. It is prose allegory, not a poem. Scholars disagree which prison stay saw the start.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Christian (The pilgrim who leaves the City of Destruction); Evangelist (The guide who starts Christian on the true road); Faithful (Christian's friend, martyred at Vanity Fair); Hopeful (The companion who finishes the journey with Christian); Giant Despair (The giant who locks the pilgrims in Doubting Castle); Christiana (Christian's wife, who makes the journey in part two)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
5. A Relation of My Imprisonment 6. The Saint's Knowledge of Christ's Love 7. Of Anti-Christ and His Ruin 8. An Exposition on the First Ten Chapter of Genesis 9. The Jerusalem Sinner Saved 10. The Work of Jesus Christ as an Advocate 11. John Bunyan Last Sermons 12. The Barren Fig Tree 13. The Treatise on the Fear of God 14. The Resurrection of the Dead and Eternal Judgment 15. The Holy City or the New Jerusalem 16. Profitable Meditation (1661, first prison book)
Publisher: Nathaniel Ponder, later called Bunyan Ponder.
Full title: The Pilgrim's Progress from This World to That which is to Come Delivered under the Similitude of a Dream" (dream allegory).
It is a Christian allegory. Its first part was written in 1678 while the second in 1684.
It is regarded as one of the most significant works of religious English literature.
Bunyan began this work while he was in Bedfordshire County Prison for violation of conventicle act (it prohibited the holding of religious services outside the Church of England).
The narrator defends the story by telling that it is framed as a dream.
He explains that he fell asleep in the wilderness and dreamed of a man named Christian, who was tormented by spiritual anguish.
A spiritual guide named Evangelist visits Christian and urges him to leave the city of destruction, because he claimed that salvation can only be found in the Celestial City, known as Mount Zion.
Christian starts his journey alone leaving his wife and children, he falls into a bog, called "The Slough of Despondence" but he is saved.
He meets a Worldly Wiseman who urges him to lead a practical happy existence without religion but Christian refused him.
Christian is sheltered in Goodwill's house who tells Christian to stop by Interpreter's home, where Christian learns many lessons about faith.
When Christian sees Christ's tomb and cross, his burden falls on the ground.
One among the three Celestial creatures, hands him a rolled certificate to enter in the Celestial City.
Christian falls asleep and loses his certificate, and he reproaches himself for losing the tickets to Celestial City.
But he eventually found these certificates.
On the way Christian, meets the four mistresses of the palace Beautiful who provides him shelter.
After descending The Valley of Humiliation, Christian meets the monster Appolyon.
Christian strikes Appolyon with a sword and then proceeds through the desert like Valley of the Shadow of Death towards the Celestial City.
Christian meets Faithful, a traveler from his own hometown, and they are accompanied by a third traveler named Talkative.
Evangelist arrives and warns them about wicked Town of Vanity and he tells them that in the town either Faithful or Christian will die.
When they enter in the Town of Vanity (Vanity Fair) they are tempted and mocked by town's people. The townsman imprisons Christian and Faithful.
Faithful rises to heaven after death while Christian escapes and continues his journey.
Now another fellow pilgrim named Hopeful befriends Christian and continues his journey.
In the way Christian rejects the means of By-Ends who uses religion to get ahead in the world.
The two enter 'Plain of Ease' where a smooth talker Demas tempts them with silver. They reject him and continue.
They meet Ignorance who believes that living a good life is sufficient to prove one's religious faith. Christian refutes him also.
Then they meet Flatterer who snares them in a net and an Atheist who denies that the Celestial City exists.
Christian and Hopeful, gleefully approach the 'Land of Beulah' where Celestial City is located.
To reach the gate into the city, they must first cross a river without a bridge.
Christian nearly drowns, but Hopeful reminds him of Christ's love and he emerges safely from the water.
The residents of the Celestial City welcome the two pilgrims.
In the conclusion, the narrator expresses hope that his dream be interpreted properly. Note: John Bunyan himself is the narrator of this story, in first person.
1. City of Destruction: Christian home, Representative of the World 2. Slough of Despond: A swamp on the way to Wicket Gate; one of the hazards of the journey to Celestial City. In Part 1, Christian falls into it and sank under the weight of his sins. 3. Mount Sinai: A frightening mountain near The Village of Morality, that threatens all who would go there. 4. Wicket Gate: The entry point of the straight and narrow way to the Celestial City. 5. House of the Interpreter: A type of spiritual museum to guide the pilgrims to the Celestial City. 6. Hill Difficulty: Both the hill and road up is called Difficulty. 7. House Beautiful: A place that serves as a rest stop for pilgrims to the Celestial City 8. Valley of Humiliation: The place where Christian is protected by God's armor meets Appolyon where Christian got the victory. 9. Valley of the Shadow of Death: A valley filled with demons, dragons, fiends, satyrs, monsters, etc. 10. Vanity Fair: A city through which the King's highway passes and yearlong Fair is held there. 11. The Celestial City: The 'desired country' of pilgrims, heaven, the dwelling place of the "Lord of the Hill" god. It is situated on Mount Zion.
In the second part, Bunyan addresses the book as "Christiana", the wife of Christian.
This part tells the story of Christiana and her 4 children's journey to Celestial City.
Christiana is accompanied by Mercy a fellow townsman.
On the way while they cross the 'Slough of Despond', they are blocked at the gate by an angry dog, but the gatekeeper lets them free.
On the way, the son steals fruit from the devil's garden and two Ruffians threaten to rape women, but they escape.
The pilgrims are lodged in Interpreter's house, who orders his manservant 'Great Heart' to accompany them to the Beautiful house.
Because of eating devil's fruit, Matthew (son) falls ill but is cured by Dr. Skill.
The pilgrims descend into the 'Valley of Humiliation' and cross the Valley of the Shadow of Death.
They encounter the giant Maul and slay him.
They meet the old pilgrim Honest and they take shelter with Gaius.
They continue their journey and kill the giant Slay-Good, then rescue the pilgrims 'Feeble-Mind' and 'Ready To-Halt'.
Crossing the river of life they kill the giant Despair and greet the kind shepherd who welcomes them into the delectable Mountains.
Christiana meets a great fighter 'Valiant-For-Truth' who accompanies them.
They cross the Enchanted Ground and meet the pilgrim Standfast.
The pilgrims are welcomed in the Celestial City.
Christiana goes to meet her maker, The Master.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Two Treatises of Government

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1689 (Sort Year: 1689)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Locke

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Two prose treatises against divine right and for government by consent.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Liberty Fund dates the writing to 1679-1683. It was published anonymously in December 1689. The title page says 1690.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: John Locke (The unnamed author of the two treatises); Robert Filmer (The writer of Patriarcha, whose divine right theory Locke attacks)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Locke wrote most of the book during the Exclusion Crisis.
The first treatise attacks Robert Filmer's Patriarcha.
Filmer had defended a king's power as a father's absolute right.
The second treatise bases government on consent and property.
It allows people to resist a ruler who breaks that trust.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Indian Emperor

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1667 (Sort Year: 1667)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Dryden

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A heroic play about the Spanish conquest of Mexico and the fall of Montezuma.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1665 matches the first performances. Wikipedia's acted and printed list gives 1665 and 1667. Britannica dates the stage success to the spring of 1665.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Montezuma (The emperor of Mexico, whose kingdom falls to Spain.); Cortez (The Spanish leader, torn between war and love.); Cydaria (Montezuma's daughter, loved by Cortez.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The play is a sequel to The Indian Queen, which Dryden wrote with Sir Robert Howard.
Cortez invades Mexico and falls in love with Cydaria, Montezuma's daughter.
Montezuma's sons fight each other as well as the Spanish.
Love and honour pull the heroes in opposite ways.
The conquest ends the old Mexican kingdom.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Marriage à-la-Mode

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1673 (Sort Year: 1673)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Dryden

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A witty comedy that pairs a bored married couple with a hidden royal plot.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1673 matches the Scott edition used by Wikipedia, which dates both acting and printing to 1673. Britannica places the production in 1672. The title is Marriage a-la-Mode.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Rhodophil (A husband who is bored with marriage.); Doralice (Rhodophil's witty wife.); Palamede (A young man engaged to one woman and drawn to another.); Melantha (A fashionable lady who loves French phrases.); Leonidas (The true heir in the serious plot.); Palmyra (The heroine who loves Leonidas.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Rhodophil and Doralice are married, but each is tired of the other.
Palamede is engaged, yet he courts Doralice, while Rhodophil courts Melantha.
The comic couples stop just short of breaking their bonds.
A second plot restores the true prince Leonidas and Palmyra.
The play laughs at fashion, marriage, and fine talk.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Aureng-Zebe

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1676 (Sort Year: 1676)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Dryden

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Dryden's last rhymed heroic play, set at a Mughal court torn by love and war.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1675 matches the writing and the stage date. Britannica says it was staged in November 1675. The Wikipedia play page shows a 1676 title page for the first edition.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Aureng-Zebe (The loyal son, based loosely on the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb.); The Emperor (The aging father, a figure of Shah Jahan.); Morat (The rebellious brother.); Indamora (The captive queen loved by several men.); Nourmahal (The empress, whose desire turns destructive.); Melesinda (Morat's faithful wife.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The old emperor still holds the throne, but his sons want power.
Aureng-Zebe stays loyal, while Morat rebels.
Indamora is loved by the emperor, by Aureng-Zebe, and by Morat.
Nourmahal, the empress, also desires Aureng-Zebe.
Aureng-Zebe wins the throne, and the play questions rhyme in serious drama.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Country Wife

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1675 (Sort Year: 1675)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Wycherley

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A London rake (a bold man about town) pretends he is harmless, then hunts wives.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1675 is the exam date. The play page dates the premiere to January 1675 at Drury Lane. Britannica also dates the play to 1675. An older life sketch claimed an acting date of 1672 or 1673.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Horner (A rake who pretends he cannot love women); Mr Pinchwife (A jealous husband who tries to hide his young wife); Margery Pinchwife (The country wife who discovers London and its men); Lady Fidget (A town wife who visits Horner under a false excuse)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
ii)
It was controversial for its sexual explicitness. This play is a comedy of manner.
There are three sources and three plots in this comedy.
The protagonist Harry Horner pretends to be impotent so that he can tricks women or seduce many respectable ladies.
He spread false rumor of his impotence to convince married man that he can safely be allowed to socialize with their wives.
By his mass seduction campaign he could identify women who are secretly eager for extramarital sex.
Horner's rumor of impotence is a great success and he has sex with many virtuous lady.
In last scene, through the well-meaning frankness of the young country wife Margery Pinchwife reveals Horner impotence to be untrue.
She reveals the truth of Horner in a public gathering. Horner never becomes a reformed character. Note: Between 1753 and 1924, The Country Wife was considered outrageous to be performed at all and was replaced on the stage by David Garrick's cleaned up version "The Country Girl".
Horner lies that he is impotent (unable to have sex), so husbands trust him.
Jealous Pinchwife brings his country wife, Margery, to London.
Margery learns town manners and begins to want her own lovers.
Horner meets the wives who use the lie as a cover.
The truth almost comes out, but the husbands still believe the lie.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Man of Mode

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1676 (Sort Year: 1676)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: George Etherege

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A comedy about a witty rake, a foolish fop, and love in fashionable London.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1676 is right. Wikipedia says it was acted and printed in 1676. Britannica says it was produced at Dorset Garden in 1676. The subtitle is Sir Fopling Flutter. The exact writing month is unknown.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Dorimant (The witty rake at the center of the love plots); Sir Fopling Flutter (The fop whose clothes and French airs are the joke); Harriet Woodvill (The clever heiress who can match Dorimant's wit); Mistress Loveit (Dorimant's jealous former lover); Medley (Dorimant's friend and partner in gossip); Bellinda (A woman drawn into Dorimant's intrigues)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is a restoration comedy written in 1676.
Dorimant is the protagonist and Sir Fopling is a marginal character.
Dorimant writes a cold note to his old lover, Mistress Loveit.
He is already chasing new women, including the heiress Harriet.
His friend Medley trades gossip and helps the plots along.
Sir Fopling Flutter arrives from France, dressed to excess.
His lisp, wig, and French airs make him the model fop.
Harriet matches Dorimant's wit, and marriage is proposed.
His reform at the end looks charming, but thin.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Plain Dealer

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1677 (Sort Year: 1677)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Wycherley

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Captain Manly trusts the wrong people, then learns who truly loves him.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1676 is the first performance, on 11 December 1676. Britannica also says it was presented in 1676. The printed book is dated 1677.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Captain Manly (A blunt sailor who thinks he alone speaks the truth); Olivia (The woman Manly loves, who betrays him); Vernish (Manly's false friend, who marries Olivia); Fidelia (A woman disguised as Manly's page, who loves him)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is a 1676 restoration comedy by Wycherley.
It is based on Moliere "Le Misanthrope".
The title character is Captain Manly, a sailor who doubts the motive of everyone he meets except for his sweetheart Olivia.
When Olivia jilts him and marries Vernish, he attempts to gain revenge by sending a pageboy (who is unknown to him, a girl in disguise and is in love with him) to seduce Olivia.
When truth of page's identity is discovered Manly marries her.
Captain Manly returns from sea and scorns the false manners of London.
He trusts Olivia and his friend Vernish more than anyone else.
Olivia jilts him and marries Vernish in secret.
His page Fidelia is a woman in disguise and loves him.
The disguise is revealed, and Manly marries Fidelia.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: All for Love

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1678 (Sort Year: 1678)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Dryden

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A blank-verse tragedy on the last day of Antony and Cleopatra in Alexandria.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1677 is the performance year. Wikipedia's play page dates the London premiere to 1677 and the first printing to 1678. Britannica also dates the play to 1677.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Marc Antony (The Roman leader who chooses Cleopatra over Rome.); Cleopatra (Queen of Egypt, Antony's lover.); Ventidius (Antony's general and blunt friend.); Octavia (Antony's Roman wife and Caesar's sister.); Dolabella (Antony's friend, once in love with Cleopatra.); Alexas (Cleopatra's scheming eunuch.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Dryden tightens Shakespeare's story into one place and a short time.
Ventidius urges Antony to leave Cleopatra and fight as a Roman.
Octavia, Antony's wife, comes with their children and asks him to return.
A false report drives Antony and Cleopatra apart, then back together.
Both die, and the world they ruled is lost.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Rover

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1677 (Sort Year: 1677)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Aphra Behn

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: English exiles chase love and trouble at Carnival in Naples.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: It opened at Dorset Garden on 24 March 1677. The Second Part of the Rover was staged in 1681. Do not date the famous first play to 1681.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Willmore (The rover, a witty English captain who will not stay constant); Hellena (A bold young woman who was meant to be a nun); Angellica Bianca (A famous courtesan who loves Willmore and is betrayed); Florinda (Hellena's sister, in love with the English colonel Belvile); Blunt (A foolish Englishman tricked and robbed by Lucetta)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Hellena is meant for a convent, and Florinda is meant for an old husband.
The sisters put on masks and meet English cavaliers at Carnival.
Willmore, the rover, wins the courtesan Angellica and then leaves her.
Blunt is robbed, and Florinda is nearly attacked by mistake.
Hellena wins a promise of marriage, and Florinda marries Belvile.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Feigned Courtesans

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1679 (Sort Year: 1679)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Aphra Behn

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Two sisters pretend to be courtesans so they can choose their own loves.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The 1679 title page spells it The Feign'd Curtizans, or, A Nights Intrigue. The database title The Feigned Courtesans is the same play.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Marcella (A young woman who loves Fillamour and pretends to be Euphemia); Cornelia (Marcella's sister, who pretends to be the courtesan Silvianetta); Sir Harry Fillamour (An Englishman in love with Marcella); Galliard (Fillamour's friend, drawn to Cornelia); Sir Signal Buffoon (A foolish English traveler mocked for his fear of Rome)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Marcella is promised to Octavio, and Cornelia is bound for a convent.
The sisters flee to Rome and pretend to be courtesans.
Fillamour and Galliard fall in love with the disguised women.
A night of masks brings fights, mistakes, and a wrong vow.
By morning the true names are known, and the right couples marry.

fields.value: The Orphan

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1680 (Sort Year: 1680)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thomas Otway

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A domestic tragedy (a sad play about home life) in which Monimia and two brothers die.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The play was first acted at Dorset Garden in February 1680. Elizabeth Barry played Monimia.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Acasto guards the orphan Monimia in his country house.
His twin sons, Castalio and Polydore, both love her.
Castalio secretly marries Monimia, but Polydore takes his place at night.
When the trick is known, Polydore dies on his brother's sword.
Monimia drinks poison, and Castalio kills himself.

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Dryden

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A political satire that retells the Exclusion Crisis as the Bible story of King David.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1681 is correct. Wikipedia lists the poem in 1681. It answers the Exclusion Crisis, the fight over who would follow Charles II.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: David (The king in the poem, standing for Charles II.); Absalom (David's charming son, standing for the Duke of Monmouth.); Achitophel (The false counselor, standing for the Earl of Shaftesbury.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
King David stands for Charles II, a king loved by the people.
Absalom, his beloved son, stands for the Duke of Monmouth.
Achitophel, a cunning tempter, stands for the Earl of Shaftesbury.
Achitophel pushes Absalom to rebel and to claim the throne.
David at last speaks, and the rebellion is checked.

fields.value: Mac Flecknoe

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Dryden

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A mock-heroic satire in which the dull poet Flecknoe crowns Thomas Shadwell as his heir.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1682 is the print date. Wikipedia says the poem first passed around in manuscript as an attack on Thomas Shadwell. The exact year of writing is not fixed on these sources.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Flecknoe (Richard Flecknoe, the aging king of dullness.); Shadwell (Thomas Shadwell, the playwright Dryden attacks. He is called Mac Flecknoe, son of Flecknoe.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Richard Flecknoe, a poor poet, decides to choose a successor.
He picks Thomas Shadwell as the prince of dullness.
The coronation copies the grand style of epic poetry.
Shadwell is praised only for being empty, loud, and dull.
The joke is that the attack makes dullness look huge.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Religio Laici

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1682 (Sort Year: 1682)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Dryden

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A plain poem in which a layman defends the Church of England by scripture and reason.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1682 is correct. Wikipedia lists Religio Laici in 1682 and says it speaks from the Church of England. It comes before his move to Rome.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The lay speaker (A Church of England believer who is not a priest. The title means a layman's faith.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The speaker says human reason is only a dim light.
He argues that scripture is needed to guide that light.
He rejects the claim that tradition alone can rule belief.
He also refuses a church that puts priests above scripture.
He asks for a middle way for ordinary believers.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Holy War

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1682 (Sort Year: 1682)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Bunyan

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: King Shaddai and his son fight Diabolus for the town of Mansoul.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database calls it non fictional prose. It is a prose allegory, closer to fiction than to an essay. It sits between part one (1678) and part two (1684) of The Pilgrim's Progress.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Shaddai (The king who built Mansoul, standing for God); Emmanuel (Shaddai's son, who leads the army that retakes the town); Diabolus (The deceiver who captures Mansoul); Lord Willbewill (A leader of the town who changes sides); Conscience (The recorder of Mansoul, damaged by the fall)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Diabolus tricks Mansoul and seizes it from King Shaddai.
Understanding, Conscience, and Lord Willbewill fall under his rule.
Shaddai sends his son Emmanuel to win the town back.
Emmanuel conquers Mansoul and restores its true leaders.
Diabolus attacks again, so the town must stay on guard.

fields.value: Venice Preserv’d

fields.value: 1682 (Sort Year: 1682)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thomas Otway

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A tragedy of love and a failed plot to overthrow the rulers of Venice.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Jaffeir has married Belvidera against her father Priuli's wish.
His friend Pierre draws him into a plot against the Venetian senate.
Belvidera begs Jaffeir to reveal the plot and save the city.
Jaffeir betrays the conspirators, then feels he has sold his friend.
Pierre and Jaffeir die, and Belvidera goes mad and dies.

items.title: "The Hind and the Panther" (1687) — John Dryden

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Hind and the Panther

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1687 (Sort Year: 1687)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Dryden

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A beast fable in which a white deer defends the Roman Catholic Church against the panther.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1687 is correct. Wikipedia and Britannica both tie the poem to Dryden's Catholic faith and date it 1687.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Hind (A milk-white deer standing for the Roman Catholic Church.); The Panther (A spotted beast standing for the Church of England.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Dryden had joined the Roman Catholic Church after James II became king.
The milk-white Hind stands for that church.
The Panther stands for the Church of England.
Other beasts stand for other Christian groups.
The Hind and the Panther debate which church holds the truth.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Oroonoko

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1688 (Sort Year: 1688)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Aphra Behn

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An African prince is enslaved in Surinam and dies after a failed revolt.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: William Canning published Oroonoko: or, the Royal Slave in 1688. It is prose fiction. Do not class it with the plays.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Oroonoko (Caesar) (A prince of Coramantien who is enslaved in Surinam); Imoinda (Clemene) (Oroonoko's beloved, also enslaved on the same plantation); The narrator (A woman who says she saw part of the story in Surinam); Trefry (The Englishman who buys Oroonoko and treats him as a guest); The king (Oroonoko's grandfather, who takes Imoinda into his house)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Prince Oroonoko loves Imoinda, but the old king takes her.
Imoinda is sold as a slave, and Oroonoko is told she is dead.
A captain tricks Oroonoko onto a ship and sells him in Surinam.
He finds Imoinda there.
They are renamed Caesar and Clemene.
A failed revolt ends with Imoinda's death and his execution.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Old Bachelor

fields.value: 1693 (Sort Year: 1693)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Congreve

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A first comedy about old lovers, young cheats, and a heart that will not stay hard.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1693 is correct. It opened at the Theatre Royal, Drury Lane, in March 1693. Congreve said he drafted it in 1690 while he was ill.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Heartwell (An old bachelor who falls in love against his own rules); Bellmour (A young rake (a man who chases women) in the love plots); Vainlove (A fickle lover who loses interest once a woman says yes); Silvia (A sharp woman who traps a rich fool)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Heartwell, an old bachelor, swears he hates love and marriage.
The fortune hunter Vainlove and his friend Bellmour chase women in the town.
The clever Silvia traps the foolish Sir Joseph Wittol.
Heartwell is tricked into a false marriage and then released.
The young couples pair off, and Heartwell stays unmarried.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Love for Love

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1695 (Sort Year: 1695)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Congreve

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A young debtor must win his fortune back and prove his love for Angelica.

fields.value: Database year 1695 is correct. It opened in April 1695 at Lincoln's Inn Fields. The database calls it fiction. That label is wrong. It is a play.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Valentine (A witty young man in debt who loves Angelica); Angelica (The clever heiress who tests Valentine); Sir Sampson Legend (Valentine's harsh father, who controls the estate); Ben Legend (Valentine's sailor brother, meant to inherit instead)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Valentine has spent his money and may lose his inheritance.
His father, Sir Sampson, wants the estate to go to a younger son.
Valentine pretends to be mad so the money plan will fail.
Angelica tests him before she admits her love.
The trick works, and Valentine keeps both the fortune and Angelica.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Love’s Last Shift

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1696 (Sort Year: 1696)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Colley Cibber

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A comedy in which a deserted wife tricks her husband back into love.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1696 is correct. Wikipedia dates the first performance to January 1696. The 1911 Britannica dates the play 1696. Vanbrugh answered it the same year with The Relapse. Do not date this play 1688.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Amanda (The faithful wife who uses a last trick to reclaim Loveless); Loveless (The runaway husband who reforms when he learns the truth); Sir Novelty Fashion (A fop of extreme fashion, the part Cibber wrote for himself)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Loveless left his wife Amanda and wasted ten years abroad.
He returns to London poor, and he no longer knows her face.
Amanda pretends to be a new mistress and receives him in secret.
In the morning she tells him who she is.
He is ashamed, reforms, and the marriage is restored.
Sir Novelty Fashion, played by Cibber, supplies the fashion comedy.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Relapse

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1697 (Sort Year: 1697)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Vanbrugh

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A second comedy where a reformed husband is tempted again.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Acted at Drury Lane on 21 November 1696. The London Stage records that night. The book was printed in 1697. The database year 1696 matches the first performance.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Loveless (A husband who slips back from reform.); Amanda (His wife, pressed to stay faithful.); Worthy (A gentleman who tempts Amanda.); Lord Foppington (A vain fop who was Sir Novelty Fashion.); Young Fashion (Foppington's younger brother, who wants the heiress.); Miss Hoyden (A blunt country heiress.); Berinthia (A witty widow who helps the intrigue.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
John Vanbrugh was the prime target of Jeremy Collier's "Short View of the Immorality and Profaneness of the English Stage". Other Major Works:.
A Journey to London: Vanbrugh had told his friend Colley Cibber that he intended in this play to question traditional marriage roles.
Cibber's Love's Last Shift ends when a wild husband promises reform.
Vanbrugh shows Loveless falling back into desire.
Worthy tempts the faithful wife Amanda.
Lord Foppington, once Sir Novelty Fashion, chases a country heiress.
His brother Young Fashion steals that match with Miss Hoyden.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Alexander’s Feast

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1697 (Sort Year: 1697)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Dryden

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An ode for St. Cecilia's Day showing how music can rule Alexander the Great.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1697 is correct for the poem. The database calls the genre non-fictional prose, which is wrong. It is an ode. Wikipedia lists it under poetry for 1697.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Timotheus (The musician whose playing controls Alexander.); Alexander (The conqueror whose feelings follow the music.); St. Cecilia (The saint of music, whose art is ranked above Timotheus.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The musician Timotheus plays at a feast after Alexander's victory.
His music makes Alexander feel like a god, then a lover, then a fighter.
The moods of the king change with each song.
Cecilia's sacred music is then set above Timotheus.
The chorus says only the brave man deserves the fair woman.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Provoked Wife

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1697 (Sort Year: 1697)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Vanbrugh

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Lady Brute suffers a brutal husband and thinks of love outside marriage.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The exact first night is unknown. The London Stage suggests about mid April 1697 at Lincoln's Inn Fields. It was printed in 1697. The database year 1697 is right.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Sir John Brute (A coarse husband who hates married life.); Lady Brute (His witty wife, tempted by Constant.); Constant (A gentleman who loves Lady Brute.); Heartfree (Constant's friend, who comes to love Belinda.); Belinda (Lady Brute's niece.); Lady Fanciful (A vain woman who plots against Belinda.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
ii)
Sir John Brute is drunk, rude, and tired of his wife.
Lady Brute and Belinda talk honestly about bad marriages.
Constant courts Lady Brute, and Heartfree courts Belinda.
Lady Fanciful schemes because she wants Heartfree for herself.
The play asks what a provoked wife may do.

items.title: "A Journal of the Plague Year" (1722) — Daniel Defoe

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: A Journal of the Plague Year

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1722 (Sort Year: 1722)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Daniel Defoe

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A London saddler records the Great Plague of 1665 as if he saw it.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The book was published in 1722. It describes 1665, when Defoe was a small child.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: H. F. (The saddler who tells the story and stays in the city)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In 1721, when the Black Death again threatened the European continent he wrote A Journal of the Plague Year to alert the people about its horror.
The narrator H. F. is a saddler who stays in London.
He hears that plague has come back, and fear spreads fast.
He notes shut houses, death carts, and pits for the dead.
Orders, watchmen, and wild rumours fill the streets.
The sickness fades, and trade slowly returns to the city.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: A Nocturnal Reverie

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1713 (Sort Year: 1713)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Anne Finch

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A night poem in which the speaker stays outside until morning returns.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: It appeared in her Miscellany Poems of 1713. Encyclopedia.com dates the poem 1713. Luminarium dates that volume 1713.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The loud wind is shut away, and only a gentle breeze remains.
A nightingale sings, and the moon shakes on the river.
Horse, sheep, and cattle feed in peace while people sleep.
The speaker feels a quiet too deep for words.
Dawn returns, and noise, work, and care begin again.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: An Essay on Criticism

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1711 (Sort Year: 1711)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Alexander Pope

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A verse essay that teaches poets and critics to follow nature and the best ancient rules.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia and Britannica both date An Essay on Criticism to 1711.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The poet-critic (Pope speaking as a young critic of critics.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is written in 3 parts.
He took three years to complete this poem, and published in 1711.
This poem was an attempt to identify and refine his own positions as a poet and critic.
The poem is a response to a question of whether poetry should be natural or written according to predetermined artificial rules inherited from the classical past. Pope exhorts his fellow poets to "follow nature".
Pope comments on the classical authors who dealt with such standards and the authority should be accredited to them as per him.
The final section discussed the moral qualities and virtues inherent in the ideal critic who are also an ideal man.
Essay on Criticism has three parts.
In the third part, Pope offers a tribute to Longinus: "The bold Longinus, all the nine inspire."
In this poem he also attacked John Dennis as "Appius" and finally a brief history from Aristotle to William Walsh. Important Quotes:.
"Little knowledge is a dangerous thing"
"To err is human and to forgive divine"
"True wit is nature to advantage dressed; what oft was thought, but never so well expressed."
"Authors are partial to their wit, 'tis true; but are not critics to their judgment, too?"
"Words are like Leaves; and where they must abound; Much Fruit of sense beneath is rarely found."
"First follow nature and tour judgment frame. By her just standard, which is still the same".
"Fools rush in where angels fear to tread."
Pope says bad critics and proud wits both harm poetry.
He tells the critic to follow nature, the shared order of life.
He says the rules of the ancients were found in nature, not invented against it.
He warns that a little learning is dangerous.
He asks for taste, honesty, and lines that are smooth but strong.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: An Essay on Man

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Alexander Pope

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Four verse epistles arguing that the universe has an order and that whatever is, is right.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia dates the poem to 1733-1734. The first three epistles appeared in 1733, and the fourth in 1734. Pope admitted authorship in 1735.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The poet (Pope, arguing for order in the universe.); Bolingbroke (Henry St. John, Viscount Bolingbroke, the friend addressed in the poem.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is a philosophical poem written in heroic couplets and published between 1732-1734.
Pope intended this poem to be the centerpiece of a proposed system of ethics that was to be put forth in poetic form.
It is an attempt to "Vindicate the ways of God to man" a variation on Milton's attempt in Paradise Lost "to justify the ways of God to men".
The poem assumes that the man has fallen and must seek his salvation.
It consists of four epistles that are addressed to Lord Bollingbroke.
In this, Pope says that "no matter how imperfect, complex, inscrutable, and disturbing the universe appears to be, it functions in a rational fashion according to the natural laws".
Voltaire called this work "The most beautiful, the most useful, the most sublime, didactic poem ever written in any language."
Jean Pierre de Crousaz wrote a biting commentary on Essay on Man, where he found that Pope had "reserved a place for him in The Dunciad".
Dr. Johnson attacked Essay on Man in Lite of Pope, "Never were penury of knowledge and vulgarity of sentiment so happily disguised."
Pope addresses his friend Bolingbroke and tries to justify God's ways to man.
He says humans sit in a middle state, between beast and angel.
They cannot see the whole chain of being (the ranked order of all creation), so they should not complain.
Self-love and reason both have a place in the design.
The poem says the proper study of mankind is man.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Night-Thoughts

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1742 (Sort Year: 1742)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Edward Young

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A long blank verse poem in nine nights on death and life after death.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica dates the poem 1742 to 1745. Wikipedia says the first part came in 1742 and nights eight and nine in 1745. The full title is The Complaint, or Night Thoughts on Life, Death, and Immortality.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Speaker (A grieving man who thinks at night about death); Lorenzo (The doubter whom the poem tries to turn toward faith); Philander (A friend whose sudden death opens the grief); Narcissa (A young woman whose death the poem mourns)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Complete title: "The Complaint or, Night-Thoughts on Life, Death, & Immortality"
The poem is written in blank verse and published in 9 parts from 1742-1745.
It describes the poet's musings on death over a series of 9 nights, in which he ponders the loss of his wife and friends.
The nine night are each a poem of their own. They are: i) Life and Death: dedicated to Arthur Onslow ii) Time, Death, and Friendship: dedicated to Spencer Compton iii) Narcissa: dedicated to Margaret Bentick iv) The Christian Triumph: dedicated to Philip Yorke v)
The speaker cannot sleep and thinks of sudden death.
He mourns Philander, a friend who died without warning.
He also mourns Narcissa, a young woman who has died.
He warns Lorenzo that delay is foolish.
He says procrastination (putting things off) steals time.
Later nights defend faith in God and a life after death.
The parts were issued from 1742, and the last nights came in 1745.

items.title: "Pleasures of the Imagination essays in The Spectator" (1712) — Joseph Addison

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Pleasures of the Imagination essays in The Spectator

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1712 (Sort Year: 1712)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Joseph Addison

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A set of Spectator essays on why sight, novelty, greatness, and beauty please the mind.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica places this series inside The Spectator, which ran through 1712. The usual exam year is 1712.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Mr. Spectator (The quiet observer who speaks the essays.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Addison asks what kinds of sights give pleasure.
He names three main sources: greatness, novelty, and beauty.
Primary pleasures come from things we see directly.
Secondary pleasures come from memory, comparison, and art.
He links good taste to a trained imagination.

items.title: "The Battle of the Books" (1704) — Jonathan Swift

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Battle of the Books

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1704 (Sort Year: 1704)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Jonathan Swift

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Books in a royal library fight to settle whether ancient or modern writers are greater.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: It was published in 1704 with A Tale of a Tub. Britannica dates that joint publication to 1704.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Bee (A figure for writers who gather sweetness from nature); The Spider (A figure for critics who spin dirt from themselves)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is a short satire by Swift published as a part of the 'A Tale of a Tub' in 1704.
It is an allegorical, mock heroic story set in the Royal Library of St. James in London.
Because of the satire "The Battle of the Books" has become a term for the Quarrel of the Ancients and Moderns.
In France at the end of 16th century a minor furor arose over the question of whether contemporary learning had surpassed what was known by those in classical Greece and Rome.
The moderns took the position that the modern age of science and season was superior to the superstitious and limited world of Greece and Rome.
In his opinion modern man saw farther than the ancients.
The ancients for their part argued that, all that is necessary to be known was still to be found in the works of Horace, Cicero, Homer, and Aristotle.
The quarrel between the books is summarized by Aesop who identifies the Moderns with spider and Ancients with the bee (who goes directly to nature and produces honey and wax which gives sweetness and light).
Aesop's verdict provokes the Moderns to attack their enemies, and a battle commences.
Under the protection of Pallas, Homer leads the ancients against the moderns led by Milton and patronized by Goddess Criticism.
Virgil attacks his translator Dryden, Aristotle shoots Descartes while aiming at Bacon while Descartes and Bacon went against Aristotelian method.
In this work Swift has used the phrase "sweetness and light". Later Arnold picked up this phrase and the title of the first section of his 1869 book "Culture and Anarchy: An Essay in Political and Social Criticism" where "sweetness and light" stands for "beauty and intelligence".
A quarrel asks if modern learning has beaten ancient Greece and Rome.
In the King's Library the books wake and arm for battle.
Ancient writers fight modern writers, and authors also fight critics.
A bee and a spider argue about true making and mere spinning.
The paper is torn, so the satire never names a final winner.

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1728 (Sort Year: 1728)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Alexander Pope

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A mock epic in which the goddess Dulness crowns a king of bad writers.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia dates versions to 1728, 1729, 1742, and 1743. Britannica names both 1728 and the revised 1743 poem. The first publication is 1728.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Dulness (The goddess who spreads bad writing and empty thought.); Lewis Theobald (The hero of the 1728 and 1729 versions, a scholar who had attacked Pope's Shakespeare.); Colley Cibber (The hero of the 1743 four-book poem, called Bays.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
'Epistle to Burlington; on the subject of Architecture' is first of four poems grouped under title Moral Essays.
The Dunciad is a satire published in three different versions at different time published in 1728 in 3 books. First version - The "Three Book" Dunciad Second version - Dunciad Veriorum.
The fourth book was added in 'The New Dunciad' in 1743. It was a reply of Lewis Theobald and later Colley Cibber replaced Theobald.
The Dunciad in four books is a revised version of first three books with a new character Tibbald. The third part never finished. Here he attacked Pedantry and Dullness as associated with boredom and sleep. Important Quote: "Thy hand great Dullness! Let's the curtain fall."
Pope first published three books in 1728, with Lewis Theobald as the hero.
The 1729 Dunciad Variorum added notes that mock scholars.
A fourth book, The New Dunciad, appeared in 1742.
In 1743 Colley Cibber replaced Theobald as the king of the dunces.
The poem ends as darkness and Dulness bury art and thought.

John Dryden published The Hind and the Panther in 1687.
Prior and Charles Montagu answered it in the same year.
They copy The Rehearsal, a play that mocks bad poets.
A speaker named Bayes reads his poem while a friend mocks it.
Dryden's white hind becomes a white mouse that eats cheese.
The joke attacks Dryden's defence of Roman Catholic belief.

items.title: "The Rape of the Lock" (1712) — Alexander Pope

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Rape of the Lock

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1712 (Sort Year: 1712)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Alexander Pope

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A mock epic about a lord who cuts a lock of Belinda's hair.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia dates two cantos to May 1712 and five cantos to March 1714. Clarissa's speech was added in 1717.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Belinda (The heroine, based on Arabella Fermor.); The Baron (The man who cuts the lock, based on Lord Petre.); Ariel (The chief sylph who tries to protect Belinda.); Clarissa (The woman who, in the 1717 text, speaks for good humour and sense.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
(1712 & 1714)
It is a mock-heroic narrative poem first published anonymously in Linton's Miscellaneous Poems in 1712 in 2 cantos.
It is also an example of high Burlesque.
It was expanded and re-issued in an addition "Written by Mr. Pope" in 1714 in 5 cantos, accompanied by 6 engravings.
The final form of the poem was available in 1717 with the addition of Clarissa's speech on good humour.
The Poem was based on actual incident recounted by Pope's friend John Caryll, Arabella Fermor, and her suitor Lord Petre from Catholic families who suffered legal restrictions and penalties.
Petre, lusting Arabella had cut off a lock of her hair without her permission and the consequent argument had created a breach between the two families.
Pope added the second edition, a dedicatedly letter to Arabella Fermor.
Pope has used Supernatural Machinery in this poem.
Lord Petre cut a lock of Arabella Fermor's hair, and two Catholic families quarrelled.
Pope was asked to laugh them back into peace.
Belinda stands for Arabella, and the Baron stands for Petre.
Sylphs, tiny airy spirits, try to guard her, but the lock is cut.
The 1714 poem adds a battle of looks, and in 1717 Clarissa asks for good humour.

The first number appeared on 1 March 1711.
Mr. Spectator and his club, led in memory by Sir Roger de Coverley, frame the papers.
Addison wrote 274 numbers, on Milton, wit, manners, and imagination.
The first run ended on 6 December 1712, after 555 numbers.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The speaker asks what the spleen is, because it keeps changing shape.
Sometimes it is a dull calm, and sometimes it storms.
It spoils sleep and fills the mind with fearful pictures.
She separates real illness from people who only pretend to be sad.
Music, tea, and company cannot drive the sadness away.

items.title: "The Way of the World" (1700) — William Congreve

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Way of the World

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1700 (Sort Year: 1700)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Congreve

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Mirabell and Millamant bargain their way to a marriage of wit and money.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1700 is correct. It opened in March 1700 at Lincoln's Inn Fields and failed at first. It is now his most revived play.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Mirabell (A witty lover who plans the marriage and the fortune); Millamant (The brilliant heiress who bargains before she yields); Lady Wishfort (Millamant's aunt, who holds the money and hates Mirabell); Fainall (A villain who tries to seize the fortune)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
6. Epistle to Lord Halifax 7. Incognita: Love and Duty Reconcil'd (only novel by him) 1. The Old Bachelor.
It is the first play of Congreve written in 1693.
Heartwell is the old bachelor who is a woman hater.
He falls in love with Silvia, not knowing her to be forsaken mistress of Vainlove.
He is lured to marry Silvia but he later discovers her true character as a prostitute.
This comedy includes the amusing character Sir Joseph Wittol, a foolish knight, who allows himself to be really married to Silvia under the impression that she is the wealthy Araminta. 2. The Double Dealer.
It is a comic play by Congreve written in 1694.
The Double Dealer is also a magazine published from 1920.
Mellefont, nephew and prospective heir of Lord Touchwood is about to marry Cynthia, daughter of Sir Paul Plyant.
Lady Touchwood, a violent and dissolute woman was also in love with Mellefont but he rejects her advancement.
Lady Touchwood finds Maskwell, a double dealer who has been her lover; he pretends to be Mellefont's friend.
He aspires to cheat Mellefont, of Cynthia and get her for himself.
Maskwell leads Plyant to suspect an intrigue between Mellefont and Lady Plyant.
He also leads Touchwood to suspect an intrigue between Mellefont and Lady Touchwood, and contrives that Touchwood shall find Mellefont in his wife's chamber.
Mellefont is disinherited and now Cynthia is to be made over to Maskwell.
Here the plot of Maskwell goes wrong because Lord Touchwood informs Lady Touchwood of Maskwell's intention to marry Cynthia.
This awakens the jealousy of Lady Touchwood, so she finds Maskwell and rebukes him.
Lord Touchwood also perceives Maskwell's treachery and defeats his final attempt to carry off Cynthia. 3. Love for Love.
It is a comedy play by Congreve; written in 1695.
Valentine has fallen under the displeasure of his father because of his extravagance, so was besieged by creditors.
His father, Sir Sampson Legend offers him £4000 only enough to pay his debts and then he should sign a bond giving his right of inheritance to his younger brother Ben.
As Valentine was embarrassed, he signed the bond.
Valentine was in love with Angelica, who possess a fortune of her own but she had not decided her partner.
Sir Sampson has arranged a match between Ben, who is at sea, and Miss Prue, an awkward country girl, the daughter of Foresight, a superstitious old fool who claims to be an astrologer.
Valentine realized his ruin entailed by the signature on the bond, he tries to move his father by submission, but fails.
He then pretends to be mad and unable to sign the final deed of conveyance to his brother.
Finally Angelica intervenes and induces Sir Sampson to propose marriage to her, pretends to accept, and gets possession of Valentine's bond.
When Valentine is in despair at finding that Angelica is about to marry his father, declares himself to sign conveyance.
Angelica reveals the plot and tears the bond and declares her love for Valentine. 4. The Mourning Bride.
It is a tragedy written by Congreve and published in 1697.
Congreve has written only one tragedy.
The famous line "Music has charms to soothe a savage breast." and "Heaven has no rage, like love to hatred turn'd, Nor hell a fury like a woman scorn'd" appears in this tragedy.
The play is about Almeria, daughter of King Manuel of Granada, who secretly marries Alphonso.
Alphonso is the son of her father's hated enemy King Anselmo of Valencia.
Almeria is separated from her husband in a shipwreck but they are united again when Alphonso, in disguise is captured by Manuel along with Queen Zara.
Manual is mistakenly executed by his own orders.
Zara commits suicide and Alphonso helps overthrow the government and publicly regains his bride. 5. The Way of the World.
It is a play by Congreve written in 1700. It is a five act play.
Act I is set in a Chocolate house where Mirabell and Fainall have just finished card games.
A footman informs them that Waitwell (male servant of Mirabell) and Foible (female servant of Lady Wishfort) were married.
Fainall encourages Mirabell to marry Millament as he was already in love with her.
Mirabell is informed by Witwoud and Petulant that if Lady Wishfort marries, he will lose £6000 of Millament's inheritance.
He will only get this money if Lady Wishfort gives her consent about the marriage of Mirabell and Millament.
The act 2 is set in St. James' Park.
Mrs. Fainall and Mrs. Marwood are discussing about their hatred of man.
Fainall appears and accuses Mrs. Marwood (with her, he is having an affair) of loving Mirabell (which she does).
Mrs. Fainall (Mirabell's former lover) tells Mirabell that she hates her husband.
Mrs. Fainall and Mirabell plan to get consent of Lady Wishfort to marry Mirabell with Millament.
Millament comes to know about Mirabell's plan and expresses her displeasure about it.
Mirabell asks the newly wed servants to execute the plan.

items.title: "A Tale of a Tub" (1704) — Jonathan Swift

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: A Tale of a Tub

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1704 (Sort Year: 1704)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Jonathan Swift

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Three brothers wreck their father's will, and Swift mocks corrupt religion and learning.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1704 is correct for anonymous publication. Britannica says most of it was composed at Moor Park between 1696 and 1699. The same book is also stored as jonathan-swift-tale-of-a-tub.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Peter (The brother who stands for the Roman Catholic Church); Martin (The brother who stands for the Church of England); Jack (The brother who stands for Dissenters (Protestants outside the official church))

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
About A Tale of Tub, Swift once said- "What a genius I had when I wrote that book."
A Tale of Tub begins with an apology followed by a letter by the bookseller To the Right Honourable John Lord Somers and a dedicatory letter to Prince Posterity.
It is a prose parody divided into sections of digression and tale of three brothers each representing one of the main branches of Western Christianity. It is in 11 sections.
The three brothers are Peter, Martin, and Jack Peter  Named for Saint Peter for Roman Catholic Church Jack  Named for John Calvin, but whom Swift also connects to John of Leyden, represents the various dissenting Protestant churches such as Baptists, Presbyterians, Quakers, Congregationalists and Anabaptists. Martin  Named for Martin Luther represents the 'via media' of the Church of England (Anglican Church)
The brothers have inherited three wonderfully satisfactory coats (representing religious practice) by their father (representing god) and they have his will (representing Bible) to guide them.
The will says that they are forbidden from making any changes to their coats but they alter their coats from the beginning.
Thus this allegory is supposed to be an apology for the Anglican Church's refusal to alter its practice in accordance with Puritans demand and its continued resistance to alliance with Roman Church.
When the three bothers inherit coat from their father, they take good care for it for seven years.
But when they fell in love with three women they proceeds to commit all types of scenes.
The three brothers want to put shoulder knot on their coats. They find some justification for alteration in their father's will.
The three brothers' story is interrupted in section 3, when a visitor discusses the nature of criticism and makes a distinction between the 'critic' and true critic.
He also discusses the difference between the ancient and moderns and their thoughts.
Resuming the story, Peter claims that as the eldest brother he is due for all sorts of titles and honours.
Peter becomes rich but has delusions about his self-importance when his brothers try to intervene; they realize that they are unable to stop his fits of madness so they leave him.
They revisit their father's will by translating it into common speech, and then they came to know what their father desired for them.
Again there is a digression here about ancient and moderns.
Peter is still rich and comfortable while his brothers are still poor but they live together for comfort.
They return their coats and their father's will trying to return entirely to their father's desire.
So they remove adornments affixed to the coat, tearing the court and thus begin to grow apart.
A lot of digression appears including a digression concerning madness.
Finally the story resumes in section 11, where jack has a very active imagination. Jack and Peter keep running into one another in the city.
Jack and Peter have teamed up against their brother Martin in order to serve their own agendas. Nevertheless, when Peter gets into trouble, Jack abandons him and vice-versa.
The conclusion declares that a work that is too long is as damaging as a book that is too short and that is there is a place for every kind of book.
A father leaves each son a coat and a will that must not be changed.
Peter, Martin, and Jack stand for three Christian churches.
They alter the coats to follow fashion, against the will.
Peter grows proud, Jack grows wild, and Martin tries a middle way.
Digressions then mock modern critics, hack writers, and false learning.

fields.value: The Campaign

fields.value: The Careless Husband

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A comedy in which a gentle wife shames her unfaithful husband into reform.

fields.value:
It is a comedy and Cibber's best play.
Sir Charles Easy is careless and unfaithful to Lady Easy.
She chooses patience instead of a public quarrel.
She finds him asleep beside her maid, with his wig fallen.
She lays her steinkirk, a loose neckcloth, gently on his bare head.
He wakes, sees the kindness, and is ashamed.
The couple reconcile, and a second pair of lovers is also settled.

With An Account how he was at last as strangely deliver'd by Pirates"

The story has been perceived to be based on the life of "Alexander Selkirk", a Scottish who lived for four years on the Pacific Island called "Mas a Tierra" which was renamed as Robinson Crusoe Island.
It is sequel to Robinson Crusoe and it is a historical novel by Defoe.
Original title: "The Farther Adventures of Robinson Crusoe; Being the Second and Last Part of His Life, And of the Strange Surprising Accounts of his Travels Round three Parts of the Globe"
The novel is followed by 'Serious Reflections of Robinson Crusoe'.
Crusoe leaves home against his father's advice and goes to sea.
A storm wrecks his ship, and he alone reaches an island.
He builds a shelter, grows food, and keeps a journal.
He saves a man from death and names him Friday.
After 28 years a ship carries him back to England.

Joseph Andrew is the brother of Pamela.

Pamela Andrews is a maid of fifteen in a Bedfordshire house.
After her mistress dies, the son, called Mr B, tries to seduce her.
She writes letters, and later a journal, to her poor parents.
He locks her in his Lincolnshire house under Mrs Jewkes.
He reforms and marries her, so the subtitle says virtue is rewarded.
