fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1742 is correct. It begins as a burlesque of Pamela, then becomes its own novel. The full title names Joseph Andrews and Mr. Abraham Adams.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Joseph Andrews (A chaste footman, presented as Pamela's brother); Parson Abraham Adams (A poor, bookish, kind clergyman and great comic figure); Fanny Goodwill (The young woman Joseph loves); Lady Booby (Joseph's employer, who tries to seduce him)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Original Title: History of the Adventures of Joseph Andrews and his Friend Mr. Abraham Adams.
It was a full length novel of Henry Fielding, and the first novel in English language.
It is published in 1742 and defined by Fielding as "comic epic poem in prose".
It is the story of a good natured footman adventures on the road home from London with his friend and mentor, the absent minded parson Abraham Adams.
The novel represents the coming together of two competing aesthetics of eighteenth century literature; the mock heroic and Neo-classical approach of Augustans as Alexander Pope and Jonathan Swift and domestic prose fiction of novelists as Daniel Defoe and Samuel Richardson.
It is written in IV books.
Joseph, said to be Pamela's brother, serves Lady Booby.
He rejects her advances and is turned out of the house.
He takes the road to find his love, Fanny.
Parson Adams, poor and learned, travels with him.
After many comic delays, Joseph and Fanny marry.

items.title: "A Dictionary of the English Language" (1755) — Samuel Johnson

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: A Dictionary of the English Language

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1755 (Sort Year: 1755)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Samuel Johnson

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Johnson's great dictionary of 1755, with clear definitions and quotations from writers.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia, Britannica, and the Poetry Foundation all date the Dictionary to 1755. This is the same book as samuel-johnson-dictionary.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In June 1746 a group of London booksellers contracted Johnson to write a dictionary for the sum of 1500 guineas.
Johnson took nearly 9 years to complete the work.
It was written in two volumes with a 10 page preface.
The title page reads: "A Dictionary of the English Language in which the words are deduced from their Originals and illustrated in their different signification by examples from the best writers to which are prefixed A History of the Language and An English Grammar by Samuel Johnson, A.M. in Two Volumes"
Number of words in the dictionary: 40,000 A Journey to the Western Island of Scotland (1775)
A Journey to the Western Island of Scotland is a travel narrative by Samuel Johnson about 83 days journey through Scotland, in particular the Island of Hebrides, in the late summer and autumn in 1773.
Booksellers hired Johnson to fix and record the English language.
He worked for years, with helpers copying quotations.
The book gives a history of the language and a grammar.
Each word is defined, then shown in lines from good authors.
He hoped to settle the language, but he saw that words keep changing.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: A Sentimental Journey

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1768 (Sort Year: 1768)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Laurence Sterne

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Yorick's unfinished travel book through France, full of small feelings and chance meetings.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia and Britannica both date A Sentimental Journey Through France and Italy to 1768. Only two volumes appeared.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Yorick (The narrator, a parson carried over from Tristram Shandy and a mask for Sterne.); The monk (A friar at Calais whom Yorick first refuses, then befriends.); Maria (A grieving young woman whose sorrow draws Yorick's pity.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Parson Yorick sets out because he thinks the French order some things better.
In Calais he snubs a monk, regrets it, and they exchange snuffboxes.
He meets women, servants, and strangers and records each pulse of feeling.
The book was planned in four volumes, but only two were printed.
Sterne died in 1768, and Yorick never reaches Italy.

items.title: "A Treatise of Human Nature" (1739) — David Hume

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: A Treatise of Human Nature

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1739 (Sort Year: 1739)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: David Hume

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The full title of Hume's early book on the science of human nature.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica and Wikipedia place Books 1 and 2 in 1739 and Book 3 in 1740.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: David Hume (The author, not named on the first title page)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The full title names the same work as the shorter Treatise rows.
The subtitle promises an experimental method for moral subjects.
Experimental here means looking at how people actually think and feel.
The first two books came in 1739 and the book on morals in 1740.
A database sort year of 1745 does not match those printings.

items.title: "An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding" (1748) — David Hume

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1748 (Sort Year: 1748)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: David Hume

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A shorter, clearer book on how we know facts, causes, and miracles.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica and the Stanford Encyclopedia date the first printing to 1748, under the title Philosophical Essays. The Enquiry name dates from a revision in 1758.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: David Hume (The philosopher speaking in his own clearer later voice)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Hume recasts Book 1 of the Treatise for a wider public.
He separates relations of ideas, such as truths in math.
He separates matters of fact, which we learn by experience.
Cause, he says, is a habit formed after repeated pairs of events.
He argues that reports of miracles need extraordinary proof.
In 1748 the title was Philosophical Essays Concerning Human Understanding.
He renamed the book An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding in 1758.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Autobiography written 1771–1790

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1791 (Sort Year: 1791)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Benjamin Franklin

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Franklin's own account of his rise from printer to public man.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia calls this his 1771 autobiography. The first book printing was a French version in 1791, after his death in 1790.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Benjamin Franklin (The narrator, telling his own rise); James Franklin (His older brother and printing master in Boston); Deborah Read (The woman who later becomes his wife)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
He begins with his Boston childhood and his short time at school.
At twelve he learns printing under his brother James.
He runs away to Philadelphia and later works in London.
He builds a shop, a newspaper, and a lending library.
He copies Spectator essays and keeps a list of moral virtues.
The story stops in his middle years and was never finished.

items.title: "Elements of Criticism" (1762) — Henry Home, Lord Kames

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Elements of Criticism

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1762 (Sort Year: 1762)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Henry Home, Lord Kames

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A three volume study of beauty, emotion, and literary taste.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That year only opens this course period. The book was published in 1762 in three volumes.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Kames asks how people feel pleasure from art.
He studies emotions such as pity, fear, and grandeur.
He says true rules of criticism come from the human heart.
He links beauty to the senses of sight and hearing.
Later teachers used the book to train literary taste.

items.title: "Elements of Criticism" (1762) — Lord Kames / Henry Home

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Elements of Criticism

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1762 (Sort Year: 1762)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Lord Kames / Henry Home

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Kames's three volume book on beauty, feeling, and the rules of taste.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica and the life record both give 1762. That is the real publication year.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
He tries to make criticism a rational science (a study based on reasons).
He looks at passions such as pity, terror, and dignity.
He finds rules of art in the human heart.
He treats beauty as pleasure to sight and hearing.
Later colleges used the book to teach literary taste.

items.title: "Lectures on Rhetoric and Belles Lettres" (1783) — Hugh Blair

fields.label: Work Title

fields.label: Author

fields.value: Blair's university lectures on taste, style, and good writing, printed in 1783.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
He began the course at Edinburgh in 1759.
Lord Kames backed the lectures, and a chair followed in 1762.
Students copied the lectures, so bad versions were being sold.
Blair retired in 1783 and printed his own text.
The book teaches taste, language, style, and kinds of writing.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Ode to Evening

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1746 (Sort Year: 1746)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Collins

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An unrhymed ode that asks Evening to teach the poet a quiet song.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The poem is Ode IX in Odes on Several Descriptive and Allegoric Subjects. That book was issued in December 1746 with 1747 on the title page. A revised text appeared in Dodsley's Collection in 1748.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker (A poet who wants a style as calm as dusk); Evening (A reserved nymph, or maid, who personifies dusk)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The speaker asks the chaste nymph Evening to hear his pastoral song.
The bright sun withdraws, and the air grows quiet.
A bat and a beetle are the only small sounds.
He asks Evening to lead him by lake, heath, and hut.
He promises praise through spring, summer, autumn, and winter.

fields.value: Odes

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Collins

fields.value: The short title of Collins's 1746 book of descriptive and allegorical odes.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: This short title and the full title name one book. It was issued in December 1746. The imprint says 1747. Poetry Foundation dates the book 1746. Wikipedia lists 1747.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Personified figures (Pity, Fear, Liberty, Evening, and the Passions, addressed as beings)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Collins planned a joint book with Joseph Warton, but the plan failed.
His own odes were issued in December 1746.
The title page is dated 1747.
The poems address Pity, Fear, Simplicity, Liberty, Evening, and the Passions.
Readers of Pope's age mostly ignored this new emotional style.

items.title: "Odes on Several Descriptive and Allegoric Subjects" (1746) — William Collins

fields.label: Work Title

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Allegorical figures (Named passions and virtues whom the odes address)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Andrew Millar printed the book in London.
The contents list twelve odes, from Ode to Pity to The Passions.
Ode to Evening is number nine.
Another ode remembers soldiers who died in 1746.
The volume failed with the public, and Collins was deeply discouraged.

fields.value: A 1779 hymn book written with the pastor John Newton.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The worshipper (The voice of the hymns, a believer praying, doubting, and hoping)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
At Olney, Cowper lived near the Evangelical pastor John Newton.
They wrote hymns for local worship, mostly in 1771 and 1772.
The book Olney Hymns was published in 1779.
Cowper's share is 67 hymns, marked with a C in early copies.
Famous ones include God moves in a mysterious way.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Poor Richard's Almanack

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Benjamin Franklin

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A yearly almanac of calendars, weather, jokes, and sayings on thrift.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia dates the issues from 1732 to 1758. Britannica dates his editing from 1732 to 1757. The last issue, for 1758, holds the preface later called The Way to Wealth.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Richard Saunders (The made up author, a man who claims to read the stars); Bridget Saunders (His wife in the early comic frames); Father Abraham (The old man who speaks the 1758 preface)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Franklin signed it as Richard Saunders, a made up name.
An almanac is a small yearly book of dates, weather, and advice.
Each issue mixed a calendar with jokes and short proverbs.
Many sayings were borrowed, then sharpened by Franklin.
The 1758 preface gathers them as a speech by Father Abraham.
That preface was reprinted alone as The Way to Wealth.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Rowley poems

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date

fields.label: Author

fields.value: Poems in fake medieval English, said to be by a priest called Thomas Rowley.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Chatterton was born in 1752. He composed the Rowley poems about 1768 to 1770. Many were first printed in 1777.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Thomas Rowley (The made up 15th century priest who is said to write the poems.); William Canynge (The Bristol merchant shown as Rowley's rich patron.); Aella (A Bristol lord and the tragic hero of the verse play Aella.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Chatterton invented Thomas Rowley, a 15th century priest of Bristol.
Rowley's patron in the poems is the merchant William Canynge.
The poems include the tragedy Aella and the Bristowe Tragedy.
A famous song in Aella mourns a dead lover under a willow.
Chatterton wrote these pieces mainly from 1768 to 1770.

items.title: "The Expedition of Humphry Clinker" (1771) — Tobias Smollett

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Expedition of Humphry Clinker

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1771 (Sort Year: 1771)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Tobias Smollett

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A family tour of Britain, told in comic letters, published in 1771.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Matthew Bramble (A gruff but kind Welsh gentleman who leads the journey); Tabitha Bramble (Matthew's sharp tongued sister, who wants to marry); Obadiah Lismahago (A proud Scottish lieutenant who marries Tabitha); Humphry Clinker (A poor servant revealed as Bramble's son, born outside marriage)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Matthew Bramble travels through Britain with his household.
The story is told in letters by several writers, not by one narrator.
Bramble is gruff in words and kind in deeds.
His sister Tabitha chases a husband and finds Lieutenant Lismahago.
Humphry Clinker, a poor man they meet, proves to be Bramble's son.

items.title: "The History of Emily Montague" (1769) — Frances Brooke

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The History of Emily Montague

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1769 (Sort Year: 1769)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Frances Brooke

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A letter novel of English lovers in Quebec, published in London in 1769.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia, the 1911 Britannica, and the Dictionary of National Biography all date the book to 1769. It was published in London by James Dodsley after Brooke returned from Quebec.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Emily Montague (The shy heroine whose love for Rivers shapes the plot); Colonel Ed Rivers (An English officer who describes Canada and courts Emily); Arabella Fermor (Emily's witty friend, and one of the main letter writers); Colonel William Fermor (Arabella's father, who also writes about the colony)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Brooke wrote the book while living at Sillery, near Quebec, from 1763 to 1768.
Colonel Ed Rivers writes home about the colony and about Emily Montague.
Arabella Fermor adds witty letters about manners, winter, and love.
The story also notices French settlers and Indigenous nations in Quebec.
The lovers return toward England, and the marriages are settled.
James Dodsley published the four volumes in London in 1769.

items.title: "The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire" (1776-1788) — Edward Gibbon

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Edward Gibbon

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A six volume history of Rome from the Antonines to 1453.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Volume one came in February 1776. Volumes two and three came in 1781. Volumes four, five, and six came in 1788. Wikipedia and the 1911 Britannica agree on those years. He later defended chapters 15 and 16 in a Vindication of 1779.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Edward Gibbon (The historian, speaking in his own ironic prose)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Volume one opens in the second century, under the Antonine emperors.
Gibbon shows wealth and order, then the loss of civic virtue.
Chapters 15 and 16 describe the rise of Christianity and offend many readers.
Later volumes follow the western collapse and the eastern empire.
The history ends with the fall of Constantinople in 1453.
He published it in three groups: 1776, 1781, and 1788.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Interesting Narrative

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Olaudah Equiano

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: His own story of kidnapping, slavery, freedom, and the fight to end the slave trade.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That year is the period, not the book. The first London edition appeared in 1789. The dedication is dated 24 March 1789. Nine English editions followed in his lifetime.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Olaudah Equiano (The narrator, also called Gustavus Vassa, who tells his own life); Michael Henry Pascal (The sea captain who renamed him and held him in slavery); Robert King (The merchant from whom Equiano bought his freedom in 1766)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
He describes an Igbo childhood in a place he calls Essaka.
He and his sister are kidnapped and sold to traders.
He survives the Middle Passage and is sold in the Americas.
Captain Pascal renames him Gustavus Vassa and takes him to sea.
In 1766 he pays forty pounds to Robert King and becomes free.
He settles in England, joins abolitionists, and asks readers to end the trade.

items.title: "The Life of Samuel Johnson" (1791) — James Boswell

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Life of Samuel Johnson

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1791 (Sort Year: 1791)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: James Boswell

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A huge biography that brings Samuel Johnson to life through recorded talk.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That is wrong. The Life was published in two volumes in 1791. A second edition in three volumes followed in 1793.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: James Boswell (The biographer and Johnson's younger friend); Samuel Johnson (The writer whose talk and character fill the book)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Boswell met Johnson in a London bookshop in 1763.
For years he wrote down Johnson's words soon after hearing them.
Johnson died in 1784, and Boswell then built the full Life.
The book weaves letters, memories, and scenes of conversation.
It shows Johnson's wit, faith, temper, and daily habits.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Rambler

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1750 (Sort Year: 1750)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Samuel Johnson

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A series of 208 moral essays, published twice a week from 1750 to 1752.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia and the Poetry Foundation both date The Rambler to 1750-1752. There are 208 essays. Collected volumes appeared in 1752.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Rambler (The essay voice Johnson uses for these papers.)

fields.value:
The papers came out on Tuesdays and Saturdays.
Johnson wrote almost all of the 208 essays himself.
He aimed to join profit and delight, as classical critics had asked.
The topics are morality, literature, society, and religion.
The style is graver and harder than Addison's Spectator.

items.title: "The Theory of Moral Sentiments" (1759) — Adam Smith

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Theory of Moral Sentiments

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1759 (Sort Year: 1759)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Adam Smith

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: His 1759 book on sympathy and how people judge conduct.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica and Econlib both date The Theory of Moral Sentiments to 1759. This is the same book as adam-smith-theory-of-moral-sentiments. It grew from his Glasgow lectures.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Adam Smith (The author, arguing in his own voice as a moral philosopher); The impartial spectator (His image of a calm inner judge of our conduct)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Smith taught moral philosophy at Glasgow before this book.
He asks how we approve or blame other people's actions.
He says humans are not only selfish.
They feel for others.
We judge ourselves as an impartial spectator would judge us.
The book appeared in 1759 and made his name as a philosopher.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Vicar of Wakefield

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1766 (Sort Year: 1766)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Oliver Goldsmith

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A good country vicar tells how his family falls into ruin and is restored.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: It was written about 1761 to 1762 and published in 1766. Samuel Johnson sold the manuscript for Goldsmith. The same novel is also stored as oliver-goldsmith-vicar-of-wakefield.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Dr Charles Primrose (The vicar who narrates the story); Olivia Primrose (The elder daughter, deceived by Squire Thornhill); Sophia Primrose (The younger daughter, who marries Sir William); Sir William Thornhill (The good uncle who first appears as Mr Burchell); Squire Thornhill (The wicked nephew who ruins Olivia)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The Vicar of Wakefield: A Tale is supposed to be written by himself in 1766.
It is a comedy novel by him. It is the only novel by him.
Dr Charles Primrose loses his money on the eve of his son's wedding.
The family moves to a poorer living under Squire Thornhill.
Olivia is tricked by the squire, and the house burns.
Primrose is sent to prison, and worse news follows.
Mr Burchell is revealed as Sir William Thornhill, and the family is saved.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Village

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1783 (Sort Year: 1783)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: George Crabbe

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A poem in two books that shows the hard life of a poor coastal village.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: It was published in May 1783 as a poem in two books. Wikipedia and the Poetry Foundation agree on 1783. He had sent parts of it to Burke in 1781.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Speaker (A poet who rejects pretty lies about country life); The Old Villager (An aged man who asks why he must live on in pain); The Parish Doctor (A hasty false doctor who scorns the sick poor); The Jovial Priest (A young minister who would rather hunt than sit with the dying)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The speaker refuses the old songs of happy shepherds.
He says poets praise country lads whose pain they never felt.
He paints his own bleak coast, with weeds, smugglers, and hungry work.
He shows the old, the sick, and the parish poor.
A careless doctor and a sporting priest fail the dying.
Samuel Johnson read it with delight before it was printed in May 1783.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Wealth of Nations

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1776 (Sort Year: 1776)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Adam Smith

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: His 1776 inquiry into labour, trade, and national wealth.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica, Econlib, and Project Gutenberg all date the book to 1776. He composed it at Kirkcaldy after his French travels. This is the same book as adam-smith-wealth-of-nations.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Adam Smith (The author, explaining markets, wages, and the duties of the state)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The full title begins An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes.
Smith wrote it at Kirkcaldy after years of travel and teaching.
He says wealth grows when labour is divided into special tasks.
He attacks mercantilism, the chase for gold and a forced trade surplus.
The book was published in 1776, in five books.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Things as They Are

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1794 (Sort Year: 1794)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is a sentimental novel by Henry Fielding.
It was fourth and final novel by Fielding (the others three are Shamela, Tom Jones, and Joseph Andrews).
It is written in four volumes.
It follows the story of Amelia and Captain Booth, after they are married. Plot:.
It is domestic novel taking place in London in 1733, which describes the hardships suffered by a young couple newly married.
Amelia marries Captain William Booth, a dashing young Army officer.
The couple runs away to London.
William Booth is unjustly imprisoned in Newgate and subsequently seduced by Miss Matthews.
During this time it is revealed that Amelia was in a carriage accident and her nose was ruined.
Booth refuses to regard her as anything but beautiful.
Amelia, by contrast, resists the attentions paid to her by several men in William's absence and stays faithful to him.
She forgives his transgression, but William soon draws them into trouble as he accrues gambling debts trying to lift the couple out of poverty.
He soon finds himself in debtor's prison.
Amelia discovers that she is her mother's heiress and the debt being settled, William is released and the couple retires to the country.
Captain Booth is jailed in London and meets old tempters.
Amelia stays loyal while poverty presses the family.
A lord and false friends threaten the marriage.
Booth's faults, not Amelia's, cause most of the pain.
A recovered fortune and Booth's reform close the story.

fields.value: 1759 (Sort Year: 1759)

fields.label: Author

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A comic novel in which Tristram tries to tell his life and is lost in digressions.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database span of nine volumes, 1759-1767, is right. Wikipedia dates volumes 1 and 2 to December 1759. Volumes 3 and 4 came in January 1761, and volumes 5 and 6 in December 1761. Volumes 7 and 8 came in January 1765. Volume 9 came in January 1767.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Tristram Shandy (The narrator, who cannot tell his life in a straight line.); Walter Shandy (Tristram's father, full of learned theories.); Uncle Toby (A gentle retired soldier obsessed with siege warfare.); Corporal Trim (Toby's loyal servant.); Dr. Slop (The man-midwife who attends Tristram's birth.); Yorick (The parson, a witty mask for Sterne.); Widow Wadman (The woman who pursues Uncle Toby.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Tristram Shandy's style is marked by digression, double entendre (double meaning), and striking graphic devices. The important characters in the book are his father Walter, his mother, his uncle Toby, Toby's servant Trim, the chamber maid Susannah, Doctor Slop, Yorick (Sterne's favorite nom de plume/pen name).
The novel accounts of the four comical mishaps which shaped the course of his life from an early age.
First: Tristram's implantation within his mother's womb was disturbed. His mother asked his father if he had remembered to wind the clock. The distraction and annoyance led to the disruption of the proper balance of humors necessary to conceive a well favored child.
Second: One of his father's pet theories was that a large and attractive nose was important to a man making his way in life. In a difficult birth Tristram's nose was crushed by Dr. Slope's forceps.
Third: Another of his father's theories was that a person's name exerted enormous influence over that person's nature and fortune with worst possible name being Tristram. Tristram's father decreed that his boy would receive an especially auspicious name, Tristemegistus but Susannah while conveying the name to the curate mangled the name and the child was christened Tristram.
Fourth: As a toddler, Tristram suffered an accidental circumcision when Susannah let a window sash fall as he urinated out of the window below because his chamber pot was missing. This accident caused his circumcision.
A Sentimental Journey to through France and Italy.
Yorick is the protagonist of this novel (narrator also).
It was a reply to an unsentimental Smollett's Travels Through France and Italy.
Tristram begins at his conception, not at his birth.
His birth is delayed until volume 3 because every cause needs a story.
Walter Shandy has theories, and Uncle Toby lives inside his old war games.
The book includes a black page, a blank page, and a marbled page.
Nine volumes appeared from 1759 to 1767, and the life story is never finished.

The play is set in Bath in the 18th century. Bath was a town legendary for conspicuous consumption and fashion. Wealthy and fashionable people went there to "take the waters" which were believed to have healing properties. Plot:.
The Plot centers on the two young lovers Lydia and Jack.
Lydia, who reads a lot of popular novels of the time, wants a purely romantic love affair.
To court Lydia, Jack pretends to be "Ensign Beverly", a poor officer.
Lydia is enthralled with the idea of eloping with a poor soldier, in spite of the objections of her guardian, Mrs. Malaprop, a moralistic widow.
Mrs. Malaprop is the chief comic figure of the play.
Lydia had two other suitors- Bob Acres and Sir Lucius O'Trigger.
Sir Lucius pays Lucy (Lydia's maid) to carry love notes between him and Lydia (who uses the name Delia), but Lucy is swindling him; Delia is actually Mrs. Malaprop.
As play opens, Sir Anthony Absolute (a wealthy baronet) arrives suddenly in Bath.
He has arranged a marriage of Jack but Jack denied saying he was already in love. Later he came to know that the marriage arranged by Sir Anthony is in fact with Lydia.
Jack makes a great show of submission to his father Sir Anthony, and is presented to Lydia with Mrs. Malaprop's blessing.
Jack confides to Lydia that he is only posing as Sir Anthony's son.
Lydia annoys Mrs. Malaprop by loudly professing her eternal devotion to "Beverley" while rejecting Jack Absolute.
Jack's friend Faulkland is in love with Julia.
Bob Acres tells Sir Lucius that 'Beverley' is courting the lady of his choice (Lydia). Sir Lucius immediately declares that Acres must challenge 'Beverley' to a duel and kill him.
Acres tells his intent to Jack and he agrees to deliver the duel note to 'Beverley'.
Mrs. Malaprop again presents Jack to Lydia but this time with Sir Anthony, exposing Jack's pose as Beverley.
Lydia is enraged by the puncturing of her romantic dreams and spurns Jack contemptuously.
Sir Lucius learned of the proposed marriage of Jack and Lydia and determines to challenge Jack. He meets Jack, who smarting from Lydia's rejection, agrees to fight him without knowing the reason.
They plan to meet at the same time as Acres scheduled to fight 'Beverley'.
At the dueling ground, Acres is very reluctant to fight but Sir Lucius will have no shirking.
Jack and Faulkland arrives. Acres learns that 'Beverley' is actually his friend Jack and begs off from their duel.
Jack now is quite willing to fight Sir Lucius and they cross swords.
David (Bob Acres' servant) informs Mrs. Malaprop, Lydia, Julia, and Sir Anthony about the duel and the all rush to stop it.
Sir Lucius explains the cause of his challenge but Lydia denies any connection to him and admits her love for Jack.
Mrs. Malaprop announces that she is Delia. Sir Lucius recoils in horror realizing that he has been hoaxed.
Sir Anthony consoles Mrs. Malaprop, Julia is reconciled to Faulkland, and Acres invites everyone to a party.
The play opened at Covent Garden in January 1775.
The first night failed, and Sheridan cut and recast it.
Jack Absolute loves Lydia, but courts her as Ensign Beverley.

The book describes the poet's visit to Hell. It is a device used by Dante in Devine Comedy.
Aldous Huxley's "The Doors of Perception" title is taken from "The Marriage of Heaven and Hell".
In this poem, Blake developed the idea of "Prolifics" and "Devourers". Milton: A Poem in Two Books.
Milton is an epic poem by Blake, written and illustrated between 1804-1810.
Its hero is John Milton, who returns from heaven and unites with Blake, to explore the relationship between living writers and their predecessors, and to undergo a mystical journey to correct his own spiritual errors.
Preface It includes a poem "And did those feet in ancient time". It became the lyrics for the hymn "Jerusalem".
Book I Book I opens with an epic invocation to the muses drawing on the classical model of Homer and Virgil. There is a mythological character 'Los' in it.
Book II Book II finds Blake in the garden of his cottage in Felpham. Ololon, a female figure linked to Milton descend to meet him. Blake sees a skylark which transforms into a 12-year old girl. Blake invites her into his cottage to meet his wife. The girl states that she is actually looking for Milton. Milton then descends to meet her and eventually unified with her. She is identified as Ololon. The poem concludes with a vision of the final union of living and dead, internal and external reality, and male and female.
Blake said- "It appears that in Paradise Lost, Book I, Milton belongs to Devil's party without knowing it".
Blake answers Swedenborg, a mystic writer, by joining Heaven and Hell.
He says progress needs contraries (opposing forces), such as reason and energy.
The Proverbs of Hell overturn the usual moral rules.
He visits a printing house in Hell and watches ideas take form.
He says Milton was a true poet and of the Devil's party without knowing it.
